newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus leaders agree to meet in Nicosia on Monday.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus leaders agree to meet in Nicosia on Monday.

text.p: Rival Greek and Turkish Cypriot leaders will have their first meeting on Cypriot soil in nearly three years next week to discuss humanitarian issues in the conflict splitting the island.

President Glafcos Clerides, the Greek Cypriot leader, and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash met in New York state earlier this month but Monday's meeting will be their first in Cyprus since October 1994.
"I always believed that just meeting and talking, having a coffee together, would be helpful in smoothing the atmosphere around us," Denktash told Reuters in a written statement.
The meeting is expected to last around two hours at the residence of U.N. envoy Gustave Feissel in the compound of Nicosia airport, deserted after the Turkish invasion in 1974.

"Both leaders agreed in New York to meet in Nicosia in between the two phases of their direct talks in New York and Switzerland," said Waldemar Rokoszewski, spokesman for the U.N. mission on the island.
"They hinted they wanted to discuss humanitarian issues. However, the agenda is very much open. Whatever issue the leaders want to raise, we will accommodate it."
A second round of talks under U.N. auspices is to take place in Switzerland between August 11 and 16.

"The agenda of the meetings to take place in Cyprus between the President of the Cyprus Republic and Mr Denktash will focus purely on humanitarian issues," said Manolis Christofides, the Cypriot government spokesman.

One hot topic will be missing persons. The Greek Cypriots say more than 1,500 are unaccounted for since the invasion, while the Turkish Cypriots say several hundred members of their community disappeared during intercommunal strife between 1963 and 1974.

The Turkish Cypriot north last weekend celebrated 23 years since mainland Turkish forces invaded Cyprus, dividing the island. Turkey took over the northern third of Cyprus on July 20, 1974, in response to a Greek Cypriot coup backed by the military then ruling Greece.
Turkish Deputy Prime Minister Bulent Ecevit, who ordered the military operation in 1974, on Sunday called for partial integration of north Cyprus with Turkey.

Ecevit said integration of the self-declared Turkish Cypriot state, recognised only by Ankara, was inevitable after the European Union gave a green light last week to Cyprus for membership and excluded Turkey.
Denktash said he hoped next week's talks would help create a better atmosphere ahead of the talks planned in Switzerland, Turkish Cypriot BRT TV said.
"If the EU suspends or postpones its decision, we can come together and talk," the station quoted him as saying.
But in the south, Christofides said there was "no issue" of suspending EU accession talks due to start early next year.
